scenes.animation: Zippy stands on a long number line painted on a school corridor floor, hopping from 0 to 1 and staring at the gap between them. The gap zooms in and keeps showing more tick marks, like a never-ending zoom.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, how many numbers live between 0 and 1? Two? Five?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Infinitely many. Today we find out why, starting from the numbers you counted with as a baby.

scenes.animation: Nested boxes build up one inside the other: 'N = 1, 2, 3, …' (natural), then 'W = 0, 1, 2, 3, …' (whole), then 'Z = …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …' (integers, Z from German 'zählen'), then 'Q = p/q' (rational). Each bigger box swallows the smaller one.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Natural numbers are one, two, three and so on. We write the collection as N.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Add zero and you get whole numbers, W. Add the negatives and you get integers, Z, from the German word zählen, which means to count.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A number r is rational if it can be written as p by q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero. This collection is Q, from the word quotient.

scenes.animation: A chai-shop glass is shown half full with labels '1/2 = 2/4 = 10/20 = 25/50' floating above it, all pointing to the same point on the number line. Then '−25 = −25/1' and '3 = 3/1' drop into box Q.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So one by two and two by four are two different rational numbers?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. They are equivalent. One by two, two by four and ten by twenty all mark the same point, so they are the same rational number.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Every integer is rational too. Minus twenty-five is minus twenty-five by one.

scenes.animation: Worked example written line by line on a green chalkboard: 'Find five rational numbers between 3/5 and 4/5', '3/5 = (3 × 6)/(5 × 6) = 18/30', '4/5 = (4 × 6)/(5 × 6) = 24/30', 'Answer: 19/30, 20/30, 21/30, 22/30, 23/30'. The five fractions pop onto the number line one by one.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Let's find five rational numbers between three by five and four by five.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: We need five numbers, so we multiply the top and bottom by five plus one, which is six.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three by five becomes eighteen by thirty. Four by five becomes twenty-four by thirty.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now just read off the numerators in between: nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two and twenty-three, each over thirty.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And if I multiply by a hundred, I get even more!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. That is why there are infinitely many rational numbers between any two given rational numbers.

scenes.animation: An 'EXAM TIP' sticky note slaps onto the board: 'Multiply by (n + 1)/(n + 1) to get n numbers in between'. A cartoon red pen circles 'q ≠ 0' twice.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: to find n rational numbers between two fractions with the same denominator, multiply both by n plus one over n plus one.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And never forget the condition q is not equal to zero. Examiners love to check it.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three stacked boxes: '1. N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q', '2. Rational = p/q, p and q integers, q ≠ 0', '3. Infinitely many rationals between any two rationals'. Zippy is still hopping inside the zoomed gap between 0 and 1.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: natural numbers sit inside whole numbers, which sit inside integers, which sit inside rational numbers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: a rational number can be written as p by q, with integers p and q, and q not zero.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many more.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I'm going to need a longer corridor.

name: Irrational Numbers on the Number Line

scenes.animation: Ancient Greece: a cartoon Pythagorean mathematician on a boat nervously holds a scroll reading '√2 ≠ p/q'. Other robed figures gasp dramatically. Zippy pops up in the boat wearing a tiny toga.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why is everyone on this boat so scared of a scroll?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Around 400 BC, the Pythagoreans discovered that root two cannot be written as p by q. It shook their whole idea of numbers.

scenes.animation: Definition card slides in: 'Irrational number: cannot be written as p/q, p and q integers, q ≠ 0'. Examples float around it: '√2, √3, √15, π, 0.10110111011110…'. A small note says 'Proved irrational: √2 (Pythagoreans), π (Lambert and Legendre, 1700s)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A number is irrational if it cannot be written in the form p by q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Root two, root three, root fifteen and pi are all irrational.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: All rational and irrational numbers together make up the real numbers, written R. Every real number is a unique point on the number line, and every point is a unique real number.

scenes.animation: Construction built step by step on a number line: a unit square OABC is drawn with O at 0 and A at 1. The diagonal OB is drawn and labelled '√(1² + 1²) = √2'. A compass centred at O swings an arc from B down to the number line, marking point P labelled '√2'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: But if root two is never-ending, how do I even find it on the line?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: With a compass. Draw a unit square on the number line, with one corner at zero.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: By Pythagoras, its diagonal is root of one squared plus one squared, which is root two.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now put the compass point at zero, open it to the diagonal and cut the number line. That point is root two.

scenes.animation: A new construction builds line by line: segment AB = 9.3 units, BC = 1 unit, so AC = 10.3. Midpoint O is marked with 'OC = 5.15'. A semicircle is drawn on AC, a perpendicular at B rises to meet it at D. Working appears: 'OD = 5.15, OB = 5.15 − 1 = 4.15', 'BD² = 5.15² − 4.15² = (1)(9.3) = 9.3', 'BD = √9.3'. An arc from B carries D down to the number line.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The same trick works for any positive real x. Let's find root nine point three.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mark AB equal to nine point three units and extend it by BC equal to one unit. So AC is ten point three.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Find the midpoint O of AC. OC is five point one five. Draw a semicircle with centre O and radius OC.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Draw a perpendicular at B to meet the semicircle at D. Then OD is five point one five and OB is four point one five.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the right triangle OBD, BD squared is five point one five squared minus four point one five squared. That is one into nine point three, which is nine point three. So BD is root nine point three.

scenes.animation: A yellow 'EXAM TIP' banner: 'Treat B as 0 on the number line, then arc from B with radius BD'. A compass character named COMPASS winks.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: to show root x on the number line, take the line BC as the number line with B as zero, then swing an arc of radius BD from B.

lines.speaker: COMPASS
lines.text: And please keep my arm steady, not wobbly!

scenes.animation: Recap board: '1. Irrational: cannot be written as p/q', '2. Rational + irrational together = real numbers R', '3. √x: semicircle on x + 1, perpendicular at the join'. The Pythagorean on the boat finally smiles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: an irrational number cannot be written as p by q.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: rational and irrational numbers together form the real numbers, and each is a unique point on the number line.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: to locate root x, draw a semicircle on x plus one and raise a perpendicular where x ends.

name: Real Numbers and Their Decimal Expansions

scenes.animation: Zippy runs a calculator on 1 ÷ 7 and the display overflows; digits '142857142857…' spill out of the screen and pile up on the floor like a ribbon.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My calculator is leaking digits! One by seven just won't stop!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It won't stop, but look closely. The digits repeat. That pattern tells us a lot.

scenes.animation: Three long divisions play side by side: '10/3 = 3.333…' with remainder 1 repeating, '7/8 = 0.875' with remainder reaching 0, '1/7 = 0.142857142857…' with remainders 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1 then repeating. Labels appear: 'terminating' and 'non-terminating recurring'. A bar is drawn over '3' and over '142857'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Divide seven by eight and the remainder becomes zero. So seven by eight is zero point eight seven five, a terminating decimal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Divide ten by three and the remainder is always one. So we get three point three three three, repeating forever.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For one by seven, the remainders cycle through six values, so the block one four two eight five seven repeats. We call this non-terminating recurring, and put a bar over the repeating block.

scenes.animation: A rule card: 'Rational ⇔ terminating OR non-terminating recurring'. Below it: 'Irrational ⇔ non-terminating non-recurring', with examples '√2 = 1.4142135623…' and '0.10110111011110…'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The decimal expansion of a rational number is either terminating or non-terminating recurring. The reverse is also true.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The decimal expansion of an irrational number is non-terminating non-recurring. Root two starts one point four one four two and never settles into a pattern.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Can I turn a repeating decimal back into p by q?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. Take x equal to one point two seven two seven, with two seven repeating.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two digits repeat, so multiply by one hundred. One hundred x is one hundred twenty-seven point two seven two seven.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Subtract x from both sides. The endless tails cancel, and ninety-nine x equals one hundred twenty-six.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So x is one twenty-six by ninety-nine, which simplifies to fourteen by eleven.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Check: fourteen divided by eleven is one point two seven two seven. It matches.

scenes.animation: An 'EXAM TIP' card: 'One digit repeats → × 10. Two digits repeat → × 100. Three → × 1000'. A cartoon kirana-shop calculator nods along.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: multiply by ten if one digit repeats, by one hundred if two digits repeat, and so on. Always simplify the final fraction.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Terminating or recurring ⇒ rational', '2. Non-terminating non-recurring ⇒ irrational', '3. Recurring decimal → p/q: multiply by 10ⁿ and subtract'. The digit ribbon neatly coils back into the calculator.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a rational number has a terminating or a non-terminating recurring decimal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: an irrational number has a non-terminating non-recurring decimal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: to convert a recurring decimal to p by q, multiply by the right power of ten and subtract.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Leak fixed!

name: Operations on Real Numbers and Rationalising

scenes.animation: A cricket scoreboard shows 'Runs: 1/√2'. The scorer, a grumpy cartoon calculator named SCORER, sweats and shakes his head.

lines.speaker: SCORER
lines.text: One by root two? I can't divide by a never-ending number!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then let's move the root from the bottom to the top. That trick is called rationalising.

scenes.animation: Two columns: 'Rational ± × ÷ rational → rational (÷ by non-zero)' and 'Irrational mixes': '2 + √3 → irrational', '√2 + (−√2) = 0 → rational!', '√2 × √2 = 2 → rational!'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Rational numbers are closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a non-zero number.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A rational plus an irrational is irrational. A non-zero rational times an irrational is also irrational.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So irrational plus irrational is always irrational?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not always. Root two plus minus root two is zero, and root two times root two is two. Both rational.

scenes.animation: Identity cards drop in one by one (a, b positive reals): '√(ab) = √a √b', '√(a/b) = √a / √b', '(√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b', '(a + √b)(a − √b) = a² − b', '(√a + √b)² = a + 2√(ab) + b'. Two quick examples write out: '(5 + √5)(5 − √5) = 25 − 5 = 20', '(√3 + √7)² = 3 + 2√21 + 7 = 10 + 2√21'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For positive real numbers a and b, these identities hold. Root of a b equals root a times root b.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And root a plus root b, times root a minus root b, equals a minus b.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So five plus root five, times five minus root five, is twenty-five minus five, which is twenty.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And root three plus root seven, whole squared, is three plus two root twenty-one plus seven, which is ten plus two root twenty-one.

scenes.animation: Worked example line by line: '1/(√7 − √2)', '= 1/(√7 − √2) × (√7 + √2)/(√7 + √2)', '= (√7 + √2)/((√7)² − (√2)²)', '= (√7 + √2)/(7 − 2)', '= (√7 + √2)/5'. The denominator glows green when it turns rational. Then '1/√2 = √2/2' appears on the scoreboard.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now rationalise one by root seven minus root two.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Multiply the top and bottom by root seven plus root two.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The bottom becomes root seven squared minus root two squared, which is seven minus two, which is five.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the answer is root seven plus root two, all by five.

lines.speaker: SCORER
lines.text: And one by root two is root two by two. Finally I can relax.

scenes.animation: A bright 'EXAM TIP' tag: 'Multiply by the conjugate: √a − √b ↔ √a + √b'. A red cross appears over '√(a + b) = √a + √b'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: to rationalise, multiply by the conjugate, which just flips the sign between the terms. And remember, root of a plus b is not root a plus root b.

scenes.animation: Recap board: '1. Rational ± irrational = irrational', '2. (√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b', '3. Rationalise with the conjugate'. The scoreboard now proudly reads 'Runs: √2/2'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a rational number plus an irrational number is irrational.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: root a plus root b, times root a minus root b, equals a minus b.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: to rationalise a denominator, multiply the top and bottom by its conjugate.

name: Laws of Exponents for Real Numbers

scenes.animation: Zippy tries to cut a Diwali laddoo into '2/5 of a power'. A sign reads '32^(2/5) = ?'. He holds a knife over the number 32, confused.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Thirty-two to the power two by five? How do I multiply something two-fifths of a time?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A fractional power is a root in disguise. Let's unmask it.

scenes.animation: Law cards stack up with 'a > 0 real, p and q rational': 'aᵖ · a^q = a^(p+q)', '(aᵖ)^q = a^(pq)', 'aᵖ / a^q = a^(p−q)', 'aᵖ bᵖ = (ab)ᵖ'. A small note: 'a⁰ = 1'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: You already know these laws for integer powers. They also work for rational powers when the base a is a positive real number.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: a to the p times a to the q is a to the p plus q. a to the p, whole to the q, is a to the p q.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: a to the p divided by a to the q is a to the p minus q. And a to the p times b to the p is a b to the p.

scenes.animation: Definition board: 'a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a', example '64^(1/2) = √64 = 8'. Then 'a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)^m = ⁿ√(aᵐ)' with m and n coprime integers, n > 0.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: a to the power one by n means the nth root of a. So sixty-four to the half is root sixty-four, which is eight.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: a to the power m by n means the nth root of a, raised to the power m.

scenes.animation: Worked examples written line by line: '32^(2/5) = (⁵√32)² = 2² = 4'; '125^(−1/3) = 1/125^(1/3) = 1/5'; '2^(2/3) · 2^(1/3) = 2^(2/3 + 1/3) = 2¹ = 2'; '7^(1/2) · 8^(1/2) = (7 × 8)^(1/2) = 56^(1/2)'. Zippy slices the laddoo into neat pieces as each answer appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Back to your laddoo. Thirty-two to the two by five is the fifth root of thirty-two, squared. The fifth root of thirty-two is two, since two to the five is thirty-two. Two squared is four.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One twenty-five to the minus one third is one over the cube root of one twenty-five, which is one by five.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two to the two thirds times two to the one third: add the powers to get two to the one, which is two.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Seven to the half times eight to the half is fifty-six to the half.

scenes.animation: An 'EXAM TIP' card flips: 'Negative power → reciprocal, not a negative answer: 125^(−1/3) = 1/5, NOT −5'. A red cross stamps over '−5'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So a negative power makes the answer negative, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No! Exam tip: a negative power means take the reciprocal. One twenty-five to the minus one third is one by five, not minus five.

scenes.animation: Recap board: '1. Laws of exponents hold for rational powers, a > 0', '2. a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a and a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)^m', '3. a^(−p) = 1/aᵖ'. Zippy shares the laddoo pieces with Neo.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the laws of exponents hold for rational powers when the base is a positive real number.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: a to the one by n is the nth root of a, and a to the m by n is that root raised to m.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: a negative power means a reciprocal.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Two-fifths of a laddoo is still delicious.
